name: 0, 1, 2, Tree!
description: Find the minimum height of a rooted tree$$$^{\dagger}$$$ with $$$a+b+c$$$ vertices that satisfies the following conditions: $$$a$$$ vertices have exactly $$$2$$$ children, $$$b$$$ vertices have exactly $$$1$$$ child, and $$$c$$$ vertices have exactly $$$0$$$ children. If no such tree exists, you should report it. The tree above is rooted at the top vertex, and each vertex is labeled with the number of children it has. Here $$$a=2$$$, $$$b=1$$$, $$$c=3$$$, and the height is $$$2$$$. $$$^{\dagger}$$$ A rooted tree is a connected graph without cycles, with a special vertex called the root . In a rooted tree, among any two vertices connected by an edge, one vertex is a parent (the one closer to the root), and the other one is a child. The distance between two vertices in a tree is the number of edges in the shortest path between them. The height of a rooted tree is the maximum distance from a vertex to the root.
input_specification: The first line contains an integer $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 10^4$$$) — the number of test cases. The only line of each test case contains three integers $$$a$$$, $$$b$$$, and $$$c$$$ ($$$0 \leq a, b, c \leq 10^5$$$; $$$1 \leq a + b + c$$$). The sum of $$$a + b + c$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$3 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, if no such tree exists, output $$$-1$$$. Otherwise, output one integer — the minimum height of a tree satisfying the conditions in the statement.
approach_summary: Precompute 2^k ancestor jumps up[u][k] and node depths in O(N log N). Compute LCA and path aggregates in O(log N) per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1950F — 0, 1, 2, Tree! [146. Binary Lifting and LCA]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary lifting for lowest common ancestor and tree jumps.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Any ancestor jump of distance $K$ can be decomposed into powers of two $K = \sum 2^j$. Precomputing `up[u][k]` (the $2^k$-th ancestor of $u$) via `up[u][k] = up[up[u][k-1]][k-1]` allows any path or LCA to be answered in $O(\log N)$.
